DOCUMENT:
Evaluation of the First-Year Peer Mentoring Scheme, 2025-26
Student Success Unit, Northbridge University, July 2026

1. Purpose
Continuation from first to second year is a key regulatory and financial measure for the University. In 2024-25, 13% of full-time first-year undergraduates did not continue into their second year. In 2025-26 the University piloted a peer mentoring scheme for first-year students. This report evaluates the pilot and recommends whether it should be extended.

2. The scheme
Students in their second or third year were recruited and trained as mentors, and each was matched with up to eight first-year mentees from the same faculty. Mentors held a group session every fortnight during the first term and were available for one-to-one meetings throughout the year. Mentors were paid £1,200 for the year. They attended a half-day training session in September covering listening skills, signposting to support services and safeguarding, and were supported by a coordinator in each faculty. First-year students were invited to opt in during welcome week.

Recruiting mentors proved harder than expected. We advertised 200 mentor posts and filled 155, which allowed us to offer places to 1,240 first-year students (155 mentors with eight mentees each). Mentee places were taken up within the first two weeks and a waiting list was closed at 300 names.

3. Who took part
Of the 4,100 full-time first-year students, 1,240 took part. Mentees were more likely than other first-years to be living in university halls (78% compared with 52%) and were somewhat more likely to have entered with higher tariff qualifications. They were similar to non-mentees in age and gender.

4. Results
Table 1. Continuation into second year, 2025-26 entrants
Group | Students | Continuing to year two | Continuation rate
Mentored | 1,240 | 1,166 | 94.0%
Not mentored | 2,860 | 2,460 | 86.0%
All first-years | 4,100 | 3,626 | 88.4%

Mentored students were eight percentage points more likely to continue into their second year. Overall continuation rose to 88.4%, from 87% the previous year.

The eight-point gap is clear evidence that peer mentoring improves continuation. Applied to the 1,240 mentees, it means that around 99 students continued who would otherwise have left. At £9,250 a year in tuition fee income, these students are worth about £1.2 million to the University in their second year alone.

Mentees rated the scheme 4.3 out of 5 in the end-of-year survey, and many commented that it helped them settle in and find out about support services. Mentors reported that the role improved their own confidence and employability.

5. Costs
The pilot cost £186,000 for mentor pay, £12,000 for training and £18,000 for coordination, a total of £216,000, or about £174 per mentee.

6. Recommendation
We recommend that from 2026-27 peer mentoring becomes a standard part of the first-year experience, with every full-time first-year student allocated a mentor automatically rather than opting in. On the pilot's costs of about £174 per mentee, this would cost around £714,000 a year for 4,100 students. On the pilot's results, it would raise continuation to around 94% across the whole first-year cohort, a gain of over 200 continuing students a year, and the fee income retained would cover the cost several times over.

7. Conclusion
The pilot has shown that peer mentoring improves continuation by eight percentage points, pays for itself many times over, and is valued by mentees and mentors alike. Extending it to all first-year students is a clear opportunity to improve outcomes and secure the University's continuation performance.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [arithmetic] at: "these students are worth about £1.2 million to the University in their second year alone" -- 99 students x £9,250 = £915,750, about £0.9 million, not £1.2 million.
2. [unsupported_causal] at: "The eight-point gap is clear evidence that peer mentoring improves continuation." -- Students opted in, and the document reports mentees were more likely to live in halls (78% vs 52%) and to have higher entry qualifications, both associated with continuation. Self-selection and these confounders mean the gap does not show that mentoring caused higher continuation.
3. [missing_consideration] at: "with every full-time first-year student allocated a mentor automatically rather than opting in" -- Scaling to 4,100 students at eight mentees per mentor needs about 513 mentors, but the document reports the University could fill only 155 of 200 advertised posts. The recommendation and costing assume mentor supply scales and never address the stated recruitment constraint (nor that automatically enrolled students may benefit less than volunteers).

REVIEW:
# Review: Evaluation of the First-Year Peer Mentoring Scheme, 2025-26

**Summary:** The recommendation is clear, but the document isn't ready for decision-makers. Its central claim, that mentoring caused the eight-point gap, isn't supported by the comparison it uses. There is also an arithmetic error in the headline financial figure, and the roll-out plan doesn't address the pilot's biggest operational problem. All of these are fixable, and the pilot data may already contain what you need.

## 1. The eight-point gap doesn't show the scheme works (critical)

The outcome data are complete and objective, as you say. The problem is the comparison, not the measurement. Mentees **chose to opt in**, and section 3 shows they differed from non-mentees in ways that predict continuation on their own:

- 78% lived in halls, against 52% of non-mentees.
- They were more likely to have higher-tariff entry qualifications.
- They were motivated enough to sign up in welcome week and get one of the places, which filled within two weeks.

Each of these is associated with higher continuation regardless of mentoring. Some or all of the gap may be who signed up rather than what the scheme did. Section 4's "clear evidence that peer mentoring improves continuation" and section 7's "has shown" overstate what this design can show.

The cohort-level figures also hint at a smaller effect. If mentoring added about 99 continuing students, that is about 2.4 points across 4,100 students. Against last year's 87%, you'd expect about 89.4%, but overall continuation rose only to 88.4%. Year-on-year variation means this isn't conclusive, but a reader will notice it.

**Suggested fixes, roughly in order of value:**

- **Use the waiting list.** About 300 students opted in but didn't get a place. They self-selected just like the mentees, so comparing their continuation with the mentees' is a much fairer test than comparing with all non-mentees. This is the strongest evidence you have, and it isn't in the report.
- **Adjust for halls residence and entry tariff**, or at least report the gap within those groups (e.g., mentored vs not mentored among students in halls).
- **Reword the claims** to "mentees continued at a higher rate" unless the analyses above support a causal statement.

## 2. The £1.2 million figure is wrong (factual error)

99 students × £9,250 = **about £916,000**, not £1.2 million. £1.2 million would need about 130 students. This needs correcting in section 4, and anywhere it is quoted, before circulation.

Two further points on the financial case:

- The comparison is £916k (if the effect were fully causal) against £216k, so roughly four times, not "many times over". It also inherits the uncertainty from point 1. If half the gap is selection, the return roughly halves.
- Tuition fee income is gross revenue, not the University's net gain. Retained students also bring teaching and support costs. Finance colleagues may challenge this, so a sentence acknowledging it would help. (On the other side, counting only year-two fees understates the value of students who go on to complete.)

## 3. The roll-out plan isn't built from what the pilot showed (significant)

**Mentor recruitment.** Covering 4,100 students at eight mentees per mentor needs about **513 mentors**. The pilot advertised 200 posts and filled only 155, and section 2 says recruitment "proved harder than expected". The recommendation doesn't mention this. Decision-makers will need to know how a more than threefold increase in mentors would be achieved, and whether pay would need to rise to achieve it, which would change the £174 per mentee figure.

**Cost scaling.** Training and coordination costs (£30k) may not scale linearly. More faculties' coordinators may need more time, for example. The £714k figure should be presented as an estimate with stated assumptions.

**Opt-in to automatic allocation.** The pilot tested a scheme for students who chose it. The recommendation is for a different scheme: automatic allocation to everyone, including students who didn't want it. There is no basis for assuming those students would get the same benefit. The projection of "around 94% across the whole first-year cohort" is the least supported claim in the report and should be removed or heavily qualified.

## 4. Smaller points

- **Survey rating (4.3/5):** state the response rate and number of respondents. Satisfaction among those who opted in and responded is useful, but it isn't evidence of effect on continuation.
- **"Large by any standard"** (your summary, not the document) is a fair description of the raw gap. Just keep it separate from claims about cause.
- **Cost arithmetic checks out:** 155 × £1,200 = £186,000; £216,000 / 1,240 ≈ £174; 4,100 × £174 ≈ £714,000.

## Suggested way forward

You could keep the positive recommendation and make it much more defensible:

1. Add the waiting-list comparison and an adjusted analysis. If the gap holds up, the case becomes far stronger than it is now.
2. Correct the £1.2m figure to about £916k and soften "pays for itself many times over".
3. Replace the 94% whole-cohort projection with a range based on the adjusted estimate.
4. Address mentor recruitment directly: how many mentors are needed, and how they'll be found.
5. Consider recommending a **phased expansion** (e.g., more places, keeping opt-in, or randomly allocating places when oversubscribed). This grows the scheme while producing the clean evidence the University has been asking for. Given the 300-name waiting list, random allocation of oversubscribed places would be easy to justify as fair.

With points 1 to 4 addressed, the report would give decision-makers an honest and still encouraging basis for a decision.
